Not E, Nonsense mutation — a base change creating a premature STOP codon (truncated protein), not an amino-acid substitution.

stem: Copy Number Variants are an important etiological factor in syndromic cases of:
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Autism spectrum disorder Why D: Copy number variants (submicroscopic deletions/duplications, e.g., 16p11.2, 22q11.2) are an important identifiable genetic cause in syndromic cases of autism spectrum disorder — detectable by chromosomal microarray.

Why not the others:
Not A, Bipolar disorder — highly polygenic; CNVs play a smaller role.
Not B, Alzheimer dementia — driven by APP/PSEN mutations and APOE risk, not CNVs.
Not C, Parkinson dementia — genetic forms involve specific gene mutations (SNCA, LRRK2), not CNVs as the hallmark.
Not E, Obsessive-compulsive disorder — polygenic; CNVs are not the key syndromic cause.

stem: A patient is instructed to name the colors in which the series of words are printed, rather than reading the words themselves. This is called the:
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Stroop Test Why B: The Stroop test measures selective attention and response inhibition (cognitive interference) — naming the ink color while suppressing the automatic urge to read the word (e.g., the word “red” printed in blue).

Why not the others:
Not A, Tower Test — assesses planning/executive function (Tower of London/Hanoi).
Not C, Boston Naming Test — assesses confrontation naming (word retrieval/language).
Not D, Test of Auditory-Perceptual Skills — auditory processing, not the color-word task.
Not E, Wisconsin Card Sorting Test — assesses set-shifting/cognitive flexibility.

stem: The Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act or 1980 is a federal law that protects the rights or people in state or local correctional facilities, nursing homes, mental health hospitals, and institutions for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. This law created a process for which of the following parties to intervene on behalf of on institutionalized person to address a grievance or complaints?

options.text: The US Department of Health and Human Services
The US Department of Housing and Urban Development

answer_raw: C. The US Department of Justice
explanation_text:
Answer: C — The US Department of Justice Why C: The Civil Rights of Institutionalized Persons Act (CRIPA) gives the US Department of Justice authority to investigate conditions and file lawsuits to protect the civil rights of people in state/local institutions (prisons, nursing homes, psychiatric hospitals, facilities for people with disabilities).

Why not the others:
Not A, ACLU — a private advocacy organization, not the party empowered by CRIPA.
Not B, State Disability Rights Centers — protection-and-advocacy groups exist, but CRIPA specifically empowers the DOJ.
Not D, HHS — administers health programs, not CRIPA enforcement.
Not E, HUD — handles housing, not institutional civil-rights enforcement under CRIPA.

stem: A patient with a history of bipolar disorder is brought to the emergency department after getting in a fight in a bar. The patient has psychomotor agitation and smells of alcohol. The patient reports not taking any psychotropic medications for several months. The patient's medical records document non-adherence to medication and previous arrests for assault. Which of the following is the single greatest risk factor predicting future violence in the patient?

options.text: Being under the influence of alcohol

explanation_text:
Answer: B — Past history of violence Why B: Past history of violence is the single strongest predictor of future violence — past behavior predicts future behavior better than any clinical or demographic factor. (The prior assault arrests here reflect documented violent behavior.)

Why not the others (all raise risk, but less than prior violence):
Not A, Past history of arrests — relevant, but it is actual violent behavior, not arrests per se, that predicts; prior violence is stronger.
Not C, Active psychiatric symptoms — increase risk (threat/control-override, intoxication), but weaker than a violence history.
Not D, Non-adherence to medications — raises risk via relapse, but a weaker predictor.
Not E, Being under the influence of alcohol — acutely raises risk via disinhibition, but past violence is the greatest single predictor.

stem: The peptide hormone ghrelin is synthesized and released primarily by:
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Stomach and small intestine Why E: Ghrelin, the “hunger hormone,” is produced mainly by the stomach (and to a lesser extent the small intestine). It rises before meals to stimulate appetite and falls after eating.

Why not the others:
Not A, Adrenal medulla — secretes catecholamines (epinephrine), not ghrelin.
Not B, Parathyroid gland — secretes PTH (calcium regulation).
Not C, Pancreatic alpha cells — secrete glucagon.
Not D, Anterior pituitary — secretes trophic hormones; ghrelin stimulates GH release but is not made there.

stem: Resolution of the process of separation/individuation in toddlers, by having an internal sense of a comforting parent, occurs with the development of which of the following?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Object constancy Why B: In Mahler’s separation-individuation theory, object constancy is the final phase — the toddler internalizes a stable, comforting mental image of the caregiver, which lets them tolerate the parent’s absence. That internalized “good parent” resolves separation-individuation.

Why not the others:
Not A, Joint attention — sharing attention to an object with another (~9-12 months); a social-communication milestone.
Not C, Social referencing — checking the caregiver’s emotional reaction for cues; not the internalized-parent concept.
Not D, Transitional objects (Winnicott) — a comfort object that substitutes for the parent; related, but the resolution is the internalized image (object constancy), not the external object.
Not E, Superego precursors — early conscience development, a different/later concept.

stem: Which of the following medications used in the treatment of alcohol use disorder is hypothesized to reduce craving in part by modulating dopamine activity in the nucleus accumbens and ventral tegmental area?
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Naltrexone Why B: Naltrexone is an opioid-receptor antagonist. By blocking endogenous opioids, it dampens alcohol-induced dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward circuit (VTA -> nucleus accumbens), reducing the reward and craving from drinking.

Why not the others:
Not A, Disulfiram — blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing an aversive acetaldehyde reaction to alcohol; a deterrent, not a dopamine/craving modulator.
Not C, Topiramate — modulates GABA/glutamate; reduces craving but not via this opioid-dopamine mechanism.
Not D, Gabapentin — GABAergic/calcium-channel; helps withdrawal/craving but not this mechanism.
Not E, Acamprosate — modulates glutamate/NMDA and GABA to restore balance in abstinence, not the dopamine-reward pathway.

stem: Which of the following types of traumatic exposures is associated with increased risk of dissociative amnesia?

options.text: Trauma caused by a natural disaster
Trauma caused by a motor vehicle accident

answer_raw: C. Trauma caused by a caretaker
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Trauma caused by a caretaker Why C: Dissociative amnesia is most strongly linked to interpersonal “betrayal” trauma — especially chronic abuse by a trusted caretaker. Repeated, inescapable trauma at the hands of a caregiver promotes dissociation as a coping mechanism.

Why not the others:
Not A, Trauma of brief duration — chronic/repeated trauma, not brief, is more associated with dissociation.
Not B, Trauma at a later age — EARLY-life trauma is more strongly linked to dissociation.
Not D, Natural disaster — impersonal; less associated than interpersonal betrayal trauma.
Not E, Motor vehicle accident — a discrete impersonal trauma, less linked to dissociative amnesia.

stem: A 17-year-old male who has been in outpatient therapy for three months reports having a long-standing fascination with fire that has led him to set increasingly elaborate fires. The patient describes feeling excited before setting these fires and a sense of relief afterwards. This has led him to frequently break curfew and, on several occasions, to steal the materials he needs to set the fires from a hardware store. Which of the following is the best diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Pyromania Why A: Pyromania is deliberate, repeated fire-setting with tension/arousal beforehand and pleasure/relief afterward, plus a fascination with fire — not done for money, ideology, or to conceal a crime. The excitement-then-relief cycle and fire fascination are the hallmark.

Why not the others:
Not B, Kleptomania — the same urge-relief pattern but for stealing unneeded objects; here the stealing only serves the fire-setting.
Not C, Conduct disorder — a broad pattern of rule/rights violations; the curfew-breaking and stealing could fit, but the specific fire fascination with the urge-relief cycle defines pyromania.
Not D, Bipolar disorder — no mood episode described.
Not E, Intermittent explosive disorder — impulsive aggressive outbursts, not planned fascination-driven fire-setting.

stem: Haloperidol metabolism is most likely to be affected by coprescription of which of the following medications?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Carbamazepine Why E: Carbamazepine is a strong inducer of hepatic CYP enzymes (especially CYP3A4). It increases haloperidol metabolism, lowering haloperidol blood levels and potentially reducing efficacy.

Why not the others:
Not A, Lithium — renally excreted; no significant CYP effect on haloperidol metabolism (though combined neurotoxicity is a separate concern).
Not B, Valproate — mainly inhibits some enzymes/glucuronidation; not the classic haloperidol-level changer here.
Not C, Olanzapine — not a significant CYP inducer/inhibitor of haloperidol.
Not D, Gabapentin — renally excreted, not CYP-metabolized, so no interaction.

stem: An eight-year-old girl experiences significant weight loss because she is disinterested in and refuses to eat a number of foods that she says smell or taste "disgusting" to her. She denies concerns about her weight or body image, and any purging behaviors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) Why E: ARFID is restricted food intake — here based on sensory aversion (foods smell/taste “disgusting”) — causing significant weight loss/nutritional deficiency WITHOUT any fear of weight gain or body-image disturbance. The absence of weight/shape concern is the key differentiator from anorexia.

Why not the others:
Not A, Pica — eating non-nutritive, non-food substances; not described.
Not B, Rumination disorder — repeated regurgitation/re-chewing of food; not described.
Not C, Atypical anorexia nervosa — still requires fear of weight gain/body-image disturbance (with weight in normal range); she has NO body-image concern.
Not D, Anorexia nervosa restricting type — requires intense fear of weight gain/body-image disturbance, which she explicitly denies.

stem: A college student drinks too much of an apple-flavored liquor and becomes very ill. A few weeks later an individual next to the student orders apple juice, and the student feels nauseated when the drink arrives. The apple flavoring represents what aspect of learned behavior?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Conditioned stimulus Why A: This is classical (Pavlovian) conditioning — a conditioned taste aversion. The apple flavor was originally neutral; after being paired with illness, it became the CONDITIONED STIMULUS that now triggers nausea on its own.

Why not the others:
Not B, Conditioned response — the conditioned RESPONSE is the nausea now triggered by the apple flavor, not the flavor itself.
Not C, Negative punishment — an operant concept (removing a reward to decrease behavior), not classical conditioning.
Not D, Unconditioned stimulus — that is the alcohol/toxin that naturally caused the illness, not the apple flavor.
Not E, Negative reinforcement — an operant concept (removing an aversive stimulus to increase behavior), not applicable.

stem: Which of the following best describes one of the functions of protoplasmic astrocytes?

options.text: Support of axons in white matter
Secretion of gliotransmitters and growth factors

answer_text: Support of axons in white matter
answer_raw: C. Support of axons in white matter
explanation_text:
Deck’s answer: C — Support of axons in white matter (I disagree: that describes FIBROUS astrocytes; I’d choose D) Key distinction: PROTOPLASMIC astrocytes live in GRAY matter, ensheath synapses and blood vessels, and regulate the synaptic/extracellular environment. FIBROUS astrocytes live in WHITE matter and support axons there.

Why I disagree with C: “support of axons in white matter” describes FIBROUS astrocytes, not protoplasmic ones. Among these options, the function specific to protoplasmic astrocytes is maintenance of the extracellular ionic environment (D) — buffering potassium and neurotransmitters around gray-matter synapses.

(Astrocytes generally also regulate blood flow and secrete growth factors/gliotransmitters — options A/B/E — so this item is imperfectly written; D is the cleaner protoplasmic-specific answer.)

stem: Wakefulness involves inhibition of which of the following brain areas?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — Ventral lateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) Why E: The ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) is the brain’s sleep-promoting center. In the sleep-wake “flip-flop switch,” arousal systems INHIBIT the VLPO during wakefulness (and the VLPO inhibits the arousal centers during sleep). So being awake means the VLPO is inhibited.

Why not the others (these are AROUSAL/wake-promoting centers, active during wakefulness):
Not A, Dorsal raphe — serotonergic arousal center.
Not B, Lateral hypothalamus — orexin/hypocretin wake-promoting neurons.
Not C, Ventral tegmental area — dopaminergic arousal/reward, not inhibited to stay awake.
Not D, Tuberomammillary nucleus — histaminergic wake-promoting center.

stem: Subjects are most likely to act as their own pharmacologic controls in which of the following study designs?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Crossover Why A: In a crossover design, each participant receives both the intervention and the control in sequence (usually with a washout between), so each person serves as their OWN control — which reduces between-subject variability.

Why not the others:
Not B, Cohort study — observational; compares exposed vs unexposed groups, not the same person as own control.
Not C, Case-control — compares people with vs without the outcome (different individuals).
Not D, Parallel group — different subjects randomized to different arms (between-subject comparison).
Not E, Cross-sectional — a one-time snapshot of different individuals.

stem: According to the World Health Organization, which of the following is the most common global barrier to accessing mental health treatment?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Low perceived need Why C: WHO World Mental Health surveys find that low perceived need — not recognizing or believing one needs treatment — is the most common barrier to accessing mental health care, ahead of attitudinal barriers (stigma, wanting to handle it oneself) and structural barriers (cost, access).

Why not the others:
Not A, Language — a barrier in some settings, but not the most common globally.
Not B, Financial cost — a major structural barrier, but low perceived need is more common overall.
Not D, Lack of transportation — a structural barrier, less common than low perceived need.
Not E, Availability of providers — a real barrier (especially in low-income countries), but globally low perceived need is the top reason people don’t seek care.

stem: During sessions, the therapist is very encouraging and gives the patient advice on how to cope with chronic mental illness. The therapist also helps the patient find solutions to improve adherence and praises the patient for taking medications. Which of the following models is the therapist most likely working in?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Supportive psychotherapy Why C: Supportive psychotherapy uses encouragement, praise, direct advice, and collaborative problem-solving to bolster the patient’s coping and functioning (e.g., improving medication adherence). Giving advice and praise is characteristic.

Why not the others:
Not A, Interpersonal therapy — a structured depression therapy focused on grief, role transitions/disputes, and interpersonal deficits, not generic advice/praise.
Not B, Psychodynamic therapy — explores unconscious conflict via interpretation; the therapist stays neutral, not advice-giving.
Not D, Dialectical behavior therapy — skills-based (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation) for emotion dysregulation.
Not E, Cognitive behavioral therapy — identifies and challenges distorted thoughts with structured techniques; the described general encouragement/advice is supportive, not CBT.

stem: What is valbenazine’s mechanism of action in treating tardive dyskinesia?
explanation_text:
Answer: E — VMAT2 inhibitor Why E: Valbenazine inhibits the vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), reducing the packaging of dopamine into presynaptic vesicles and thus dopamine release. This dampens the dopaminergic hypersensitivity underlying tardive dyskinesia. (Deutetrabenazine and tetrabenazine share this mechanism.)

Why not the others:
Not A, D2 inverse agonist — not valbenazine’s mechanism.
Not B, NMDA antagonist — e.g., amantadine/memantine, not valbenazine.
Not C, M1 antagonist — anticholinergics (can actually worsen TD), not valbenazine.
Not D, GABA agonist — e.g., benzodiazepines, not valbenazine’s mechanism.

stem: Which of the following exam findings suggests a non-organic etiology for a patient complaining of leg weakness?

options.text: Slow movements of the toes associated with rigid tone
Loss of sensation to pinprick but preserved vibration sensation
Hyperreflexia and increased tone with an upgoing toe on one side
Pressing down with the paretic leg when asked to raise the unaffected leg
Limitation in dorsiflexion of the leg with decreased sensation over the anterior foot

answer_text: Pressing down with the paretic leg when asked to raise the unaffected leg
answer_raw: D. Pressing down with the paretic leg when asked to raise the unaffected leg
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Downward pressure in the “weak” leg when raising the good leg (Hoover’s sign) Why D: This describes Hoover’s sign. In functional (non-organic) leg weakness, asking the patient to raise the UNAFFECTED leg produces involuntary downward pressure (hip extension) in the “weak” leg — showing that leg can actually move normally. That inconsistency indicates a functional cause.

Why not the others (these suggest ORGANIC pathology):
Not A, Slow movements with rigid tone — parkinsonian/organic.
Not B, Loss of pinprick but preserved vibration — a dissociated sensory loss (organic spinothalamic pattern).
Not C, Hyperreflexia and increased tone with an upgoing toe — upper motor neuron (organic) signs.
Not E, Limited dorsiflexion with decreased sensation over the anterior foot — a peroneal nerve/L5 (organic) pattern.

stem: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which forms the legal basis for the interventions commonly known as "504 plans," ensures which of the following for students with disabilities?

options.text: Accommodations necessary to meet educational needs
Separate classrooms for students with significant needs
Access to supportive services throughout the calendar year
Out of district placement when a school cannot meet a child's needs

answer_text: Accommodations necessary to meet educational needs
answer_raw: B. Accommodations necessary to meet educational needs
explanation_text:
Answer: B — Accommodations necessary to meet educational needs Why B: Section 504 prohibits disability discrimination and requires schools to provide ACCOMMODATIONS so students with disabilities can access education on an equal basis (e.g., extra time, preferential seating). It guarantees accommodations to meet educational needs.

Why not the others (these belong to IDEA/IEP, not 504):
Not A, Multidisciplinary assessment — a feature of the IDEA/IEP eligibility process.
Not C, Separate classrooms — 504 emphasizes access in the general setting, not segregation.
Not D, Year-round services — extended-school-year services relate to IEPs.
Not E, Out-of-district placement — an IDEA/IEP provision when a district can’t meet needs.

stem: A resident physician creates an online social media account for networking and personal use. Which of the following is the best behavior to maintain professionalism while online?

options.text: Check the online profile regularly for accuracy
Accept or send friend requests to former patients

answer_text: Check the online profile regularly for accuracy
answer_raw: C. Check the online profile regularly for accuracy
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Check the online profile regularly for accuracy Why C: Online professionalism means actively managing your digital footprint — regularly checking your profile for accuracy and for content others may post about you, keeping it consistent with professional standards.

Why not the others:
Not A, Set privacy settings to “public” — settings should be restrictive/private, not public.
Not B, Share stories about difficult patients — a confidentiality violation; never appropriate.
Not D, Friend former patients — a boundary violation (dual relationship) to be avoided.

stem: A parent brings a child for care for anxiety about attending school. The parent and child have a loving relationship and the parent allows the child to stay home from school whenever the child’s anxiety is high. This parenting style can best be classified as:
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Permissive Why C: Permissive parenting (Baumrind) is high in warmth/responsiveness but low in demands/limit-setting. A loving parent who accommodates the child by allowing school avoidance — without enforcing firm expectations — fits permissive.

Why not the others:
Not A, Chaotic — inconsistent/unstructured; not a standard Baumrind style, and the warmth here is consistent.
Not B, Detached (neglectful) — low warmth AND low demands; this parent is loving (high warmth).
Not D, Authoritative — high warmth AND high, consistent expectations/limits; this parent is not setting firm limits.

stem: Between which Tanner stages can a girl become pregnant?
explanation_text:
Deck shows two answers (C and D) — I’d go with C (3 to 4) Key fact: a girl can ovulate — and therefore conceive — BEFORE her first period (menarche), which typically occurs at Tanner stage 4. So fertility can begin around the stage 3-to-4 transition.

Why I’d pick C (3 to 4): because ovulation can precede menarche, pregnancy becomes biologically possible before the first menstrual period — i.e., during the move from stage 3 to 4.

Why the deck also lists D (4 to 5): if you tie fertility strictly to menarche (stage 4) and established ovulatory cycles (stage 5), the window shifts later. But since conception can occur before menarche, C is the more complete answer.

stem: In writing progress notes, which of the following describes the recommended use of the "cloning” or “copy forward" function in the electronic medical record?

options.text: Data copied forward should be kept in an unmodified form.
Cloning should be routinely used to improve billings and increase payments.
Data copied forward should be essential and pertinent to the current encounter.
Laboratory and imaging data are the only sections that should be copied forward.

answer_text: Data copied forward should be essential and pertinent to the current owner
answer_raw: C. Data copied forward should be essential and pertinent to the current owner
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Copied data should be essential and pertinent to the current encounter Why C: When using copy-forward/cloning, only information that is essential and pertinent to the CURRENT encounter should be carried over (and updated). Blindly propagating stale data creates inaccurate, bloated, misleading notes.

Why not the others:
Not A, Kept unmodified — copied data must be reviewed and UPDATED for the current visit, not left untouched.
Not B, Used to improve billings/payments — cloning to inflate billing is fraudulent and inappropriate.
Not D, Only labs and imaging copied forward — there is no such fixed-section rule; the guiding principle is relevance to the current encounter.

stem: Which of the following factors contributed to the failure of the early Genome-wide Association Studies to identify any risk variants for psychiatric disorders?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Sample size Why A: Psychiatric disorders are highly polygenic — many common variants, each with a tiny effect size. Early GWAS were underpowered (sample sizes too small) to reach genome-wide significance for such small effects. Only large consortia with very large samples succeeded.

Why not the others:
Not B, High co-morbidity — a real complication in psychiatry, but not the principal reason early GWAS failed.
Not C, DSM nomenclature — diagnostic heterogeneity adds noise, but sample size was the limiting factor.
Not D, Population stratification — a confounder that can be corrected statistically; not the main cause of early failure.

stem: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex plays an important role in which of the following activities?
explanation_text:
Answer: A — Working memory Why A: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) is the classic seat of working memory and executive function — holding and manipulating information “online” for reasoning and planning.

Why not the others:
Not B, Long-term memory — depends on the medial temporal lobe/hippocampus, not the DLPFC.
Not C, Visuospatial perception — a parietal (and occipital) function.
Not D, Smooth-pursuit eye movement — involves the frontal/parietal eye fields, cerebellum, and brainstem, not DLPFC working-memory circuits.

stem: A patient reports smoking cigarettes daily for several years, expresses the desire to stop smoking, but is fearful after unsuccessful attempts in the past. Using motivational interviewing, which of the following would be the best statement to make next?

options.text: "You mentioned that you smoke every day. How much do you smoke?"
"You tried to stop before, but it didn't work. What's different about this time?"
"Has anyone talked to you about medication options to help you quit smoking?"
"Quitting smoking can be very hard. What do you think is the hardest part of quitting?"

answer_text: “Quitting smoking can be very hard. What do you think is the hardest part of quitting?”
answer_raw: D. “Quitting smoking can be very hard. What do you think is the hardest part of quitting?”
explanation_text:
Answer: D — “Quitting smoking can be very hard. What do you think is the hardest part of quitting?” Why D: Motivational interviewing emphasizes empathy and open-ended, patient-centered exploration. D validates the difficulty (empathy) and invites the patient to explore his own barriers with an open-ended question — the core MI spirit.

Why not the others:
Not A, “How much do you smoke?” — a closed, information-gathering question, not the empathic change-focused MI approach.
Not B, “What’s different this time?” — reasonable, but feels confrontational given his fear of failure; less empathic than D.
Not C, “Has anyone talked to you about medication?” — jumps to advice/solutions prematurely, against MI’s elicit-before-inform style.

stem: A female patient with Bipolar Disorder Type I is stable on a combination of lithium 900mg daily and lamotrigine 200mg daily. During an encounter she reports the recent initiation of a combined oral contraceptive pill by the PCP. Which of the following potential issues with the use of this type of OCP is important to discuss with the patient during the visit?

options.text: The OCP may necessitate a dose increase in lithium.
The OCP may necessitate a dose increase in lamotrigine.
The OCP may not be effective when taken in combination with lithium.
The OCP may not be effective when taken in combination with lamotrigine.

answer_text: The OCP may necessitate a dose increase in lamotrigine
answer_raw: B. The OCP may necessitate a dose increase in lamotrigine
explanation_text:
Answer: B — The OCP may necessitate a dose increase in lamotrigine Why B: Estrogen-containing OCPs induce glucuronidation (UGT1A4), which increases lamotrigine clearance and LOWERS its level (often by about half). The lamotrigine dose may need to be raised to stay effective — and watch for toxicity during the pill-free week, when levels rebound.

Why not the others:
Not A, Dose increase in lithium — lithium is renally excreted and not significantly affected by OCPs.
Not C, OCP ineffective with lithium — lithium doesn’t induce hepatic enzymes, so it doesn’t reduce OCP efficacy.
Not D, OCP ineffective with lamotrigine — lamotrigine is not an enzyme inducer and doesn’t meaningfully reduce contraceptive efficacy; the interaction runs the other way (OCP lowers lamotrigine).

stem: Which of the following is typical of the course of migraine headache disorder during pregnancy?

options.text: Improves during the second and third trimester
Is associated with increased risk of miscarriage

answer_text: Improves during the second and third trimester
answer_raw: C. Improves during the second and third trimester
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Improves during the second and third trimester Why C: Migraines (especially migraine WITHOUT aura) tend to IMPROVE during pregnancy, most notably in the second and third trimesters, thanks to sustained high, stable estrogen levels.

Why not the others:
Not A, No significant change — most patients actually experience improvement.
Not B, Worsens in the first trimester — early pregnancy is variable, but the characteristic course is later improvement, not first-trimester worsening.
Not D, Increased risk of miscarriage — migraine itself isn’t linked to miscarriage (though severe migraine relates to other vascular risks like preeclampsia).

stem: Most known drugs of abuse activate which of the following dopaminergic pathways, leading to addictive behavior?
explanation_text:
Answer: C — Mesoaccumbens (mesolimbic) Why C: The mesoaccumbens (mesolimbic) pathway runs from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens — the brain’s reward circuit. Nearly all drugs of abuse raise dopamine here, reinforcing addictive behavior.

Why not the others:
Not A, Nigrostriatal — substantia nigra to striatum; controls movement (degenerates in Parkinson’s), not reward.
Not B, Mesocortical — VTA to prefrontal cortex; involved in cognition/motivation (and negative symptoms), not the primary reward-reinforcement site.
Not D, Tuberohypophyseal (tuberoinfundibular) — hypothalamus to pituitary; regulates prolactin, unrelated to addiction.

stem: Which of the following best describes how imprinting can lead to expression of a disease phenotype?

options.text: Acetylation of histones leads to altered chromosome packaging.
Maternally inherited transcription factors prevent the expression of paternal alleles.
Methylation of a chromosome leads to overexpression of all genes on the same chromosome.
Methylation of the paternal or maternal allele leads to unopposed expression of the other allele.

answer_text: Methylation of the paternal or maternal allele leads to unopposed expression of the other allele
answer_raw: D. Methylation of the paternal or maternal allele leads to unopposed expression of the other allele.
explanation_text:
Answer: D — Methylation of one parental allele leaves the other allele’s expression unopposed Why D: Genomic imprinting silences one parental copy of a gene via methylation, leaving only the OTHER parent’s allele expressed (“unopposed”). If that single active allele is defective (mutated/deleted), disease results — the classic example is Prader-Willi vs Angelman syndrome (same 15q deletion, different parent of origin).

Why not the others:
Not A, Histone acetylation altering packaging — a general epigenetic mechanism, but doesn’t capture the parent-of-origin allele silencing that defines imprinting.
Not B, Maternal transcription factors blocking paternal alleles — imprinting works through DNA methylation marks, not inherited transcription factors.
Not C, Methylation overexpressing all genes on a chromosome — methylation generally SILENCES genes and is locus/allele-specific, not whole-chromosome overexpression.

stem: When measuring personality traits, which of the following are advantages of psychometric testing over the clinical interview? (Select three)

options.text: Ability to measure question response patterns
Elimination of bias based on ideological orientation

answer_text: Ability to measure validity F. Ability to measure question response patterns H. Elimination of bias based on ideological orientation
answer_raw: A. Ability to measure validity F. Ability to measure question response patterns H. Elimination of bias based on ideological orientation
explanation_text:
Answer: A, F, H (select three) Why these three:
A, Measure validity — standardized tests have established validity/norms; a clinical interview can’t quantify it.
F, Measure response patterns — tests include validity scales that detect response styles (inconsistency, faking good/bad) an interview can’t systematically capture.
H, Eliminate ideological bias — standardized scoring removes the examiner’s personal/ideological bias that colors an interview.

Why not the others:
Not B, Patient reliability — tests improve measurement reliability, not the patient’s truthfulness.
Not C, Reduce self-reporting bias — most tests still rely on self-report, so this bias isn’t eliminated.
Not D, Minimize defensive responses — defensiveness still occurs (validity scales may flag it).
Not E, Less need for collateral — testing doesn’t reduce the need for collateral history.
Not G, Ego-dystonic behavior — not a recognized specific advantage of testing.

stem: Studies of psychotherapy intervention consistently find which of the following therapist variables most closely correlated with a positive therapeutic alliance? (Select three)
answer_text: Genuineness D. Empathy for patient E. Unconditional warmth
answer_raw: C. Genuineness D. Empathy for patient E. Unconditional warmth
explanation_text:
Answer: C, D, E (select three) — Rogers’ core conditions Why these three (Carl Rogers’ core therapeutic conditions, the strongest predictors of alliance):
C, Genuineness (congruence) — the therapist being authentic builds trust.
D, Empathy — accurately understanding the patient’s experience strengthens the bond.
E, Unconditional warmth (positive regard) — nonjudgmental acceptance fosters alliance.

Why not the others (therapist demographics and specific technique aren’t reliably linked to alliance):
Not A, Gender — doesn’t reliably predict alliance.
Not B, Older age — not a consistent predictor.
Not F, Therapeutic approach — the relationship matters more than the specific modality (common-factors finding).
Not G, Similar ethnic background — matching isn’t required for strong alliance.
Not H, Similar socioeconomic status — likewise not a reliable predictor.
